Gqeberha Gangs

By: Chuma Kave | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Violent house robberies have community under siege

Summary:
THE NB GANGS

The community of Despatch, a small town just outside of Gqeberha in the Eastern Cape, sleeps with one eye open, living in fear as the notorious gang known as The Panga Gang has been terrorising them for months. They are known for striking in the early hours (between 2 am and 4 am) more especially during load shedding making off with home appliances and cell phones. Before, they used to carry pangas and screwdrivers but off late, they have added firearms.

The Panga Gang is also accused or suspected of being responsible for the recent break-in at an old-age home in Bluewater Bay where two people were murdered and the killers making off with four phones, jewellery and two TV sets. Despatch is a community of just over 50 000 people with one police van. They describe the town as one of the most peaceful but now it expereinces at least 16 break-ins a week and shoes with shootings. The communities have now formed countless patrol groups and hit the streets every night and also use social media to alert the communities. They are installing cameras and some acquiring their own weapons.

Headlines splashed in the local newspapers include “Robbery gangs strike fear in Nelson Mandela Bay”, “Robbery gangs target western suburbs”, “Panga Gang or copycats branching out into Despatch”

However, this hasn’t discouraged the criminals and instead gave birth to two more gangs, The Balaclava Gang and the Quantum gang victimising the same neighbourhoods.

This trend 2 am break-ins is currently spreading all over the Nelson Mandela Bay and has now included other towns like Kariega (Uitenhage), Bluewater Bay and other parts of Gqeberha. the story to investigate how this shocked community is dealing with this and steps they have taken to protect themselves.

DARRLY Opperman
Ryno Matthyesen

Press Release:


Gangs of Gqeberha
In the town of Despatch in the Eastern Cape, residents sleep with one eye open. On most nights, brazen robbers wielding pangas and guns stalk their streets, breaking in and terrorising the community in their homes. But are these just opportunistic criminals or are they recruits from gangs entrenched in Gqeberha’s inner city? From drug dealing to gun smuggling, the biggest city in the Eastern Cape has long been wracked by criminal enterprises vying for turf. Now, similarly violent operators are making the rural outskirts their stronghold. As residents and private security companies fight back, Carte Blanche investigates why this community has become such an easy target.

Producer: Chuma Kave | Presenter: Govan Whittles

Script:


They prowl in the dead of night: two or three masked men, picking out the quiet streets. Dodging lights.. dogs.. private security.. until they manage to creep.. or shoot their way inside..

VOICENOTE SUBS: Please help… they’ve shot him in the stomach… I don’t have much experience with that - please help.

Hitting soft targets - but armed and dangerous.

VOICENOTE SUBS: I just want to let you know that we’re here at the hospital… his blood pressure has dropped a lot. Thank you very much for everyone’s help - all I’m asking for are prayers, please. Please.

The streets of Despatch tell a disturbing story: until recently there were few high walls or high-tech security here…
Segue to Ryno
It was a sleepy suburban town on Nelson Mandela Bay’s rural fringes when Ryno Matthysen grew up here - and so last year he bought a house with his girlfriend close to his parents’ home. Within months, they were hit twice.

RYNO: I just shouted at them… a life’s worth nothing anymore.. I grabbed a knife.. Hunting rifle was still in the safe.. Tried to protect myself.. When I shouted them.. Perfect shot to my heart…

What Ryno thought was perfectly adequate security with the open veld across the road, he now stepped up a notch.

RYNO: my girlfriend is taking it quite badly .. can’t sleep…have done the electric fencing.. Put in cameras - nothing I can do.

Across the suburb, the safety Darryl Opperman had always taken for granted was shattered last June with two home invasions, two nights in a row. Robbers pistolwhipped her husband, looking for electronics.

GOVAN How is your husband doing now?
DARRYL: I think we're doing better … last night I woke up and one of the things other people said they heard is they hear them whistling. That's the way they communicate. They whistle.
GOVAN: So it sounds like this community is on edge.
DARRYL: Yes. You don't want to look through the windows that they can see you if they are there. My dog started barking so there is something there.
By now - like many in Despatch - the Oppermans have installed an alarm system with armed response.
DARRYL: So you sitting there with the panic button and waiting.
And this is what the area’s CCTV cameras and private security companies are capturing - night, after night… after night.

TRANSITION

The Bay’s beautiful ocean does little to ease the tension that’s palpable under the surface.

LINK GOVAN: Just look at this - if you had to take a look at this you’d swear that this is one of the best cities in South Africa - this is made for tourism. Instead - NMB is infested with gangs and unlike Cape Town the gangs aren’t isolated to one area.

The local Herald Newspaper’s headlines have tracked the spread of house robberies from the inner city to the outskirts: the latest spike coinciding with the easing of COVID-19 lockdowns and their brutal financial impact on the city. Riaan Marais is senior reporter.
GOVAN: And so how did it start?
RIAAN: So we initially had a group that sort of earned the name the Balaclava gang. They were between 2 and 4 guys hitting all the properties around the outskirts of the city. But these guys were known for always wearing masks. The other one, known to be one of the quite violent gangs is the Panga Gang, because they use Pangas during the commission of their crimes. Another one is in the name of the quantum gang because there seems to be. Whenever these incidents happen, there's a Toyota Quantum minibus in the area seemingly picking these guys up once they've committed these crimes.
GOVAN: Riaan, that sounds incredibly scary. The names already strike fear into me…
RIAAN: Look, these guys feed on that kind of fear. They feed on this reputation.
GOVAN: Robberies happen all the time across the country, right? But what is it about these robberies that sets them apart from what we've seen before?
RIAAN: I think it's the frequency with which they happen. It's not like, oh, you hear about it. And then 2 or 3 weeks later, it happens again. These are like once or twice a week, you know, some of them hitting three times a week, you know, in the same area.
A decade ago the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organised Crime said there were two main gangs with 33 affiliates at work in the Bay - on every criminal enterprise from drug trafficking to extortion to firearms to robberies.

In a northern suburb notorious for gangsterism, we ask to meet Julian Julies - a former general with a prison gang, who claims to have turned his life around.

UPS greeting

Julian says the robbery gangs are not working for themselves.

JULIAN: They get recruited innocently in getting involved because there is a syndicate operating in the city there's inner circle and outer circle. Now, the inner circle is where the syndicate operations are taking place, where the money is speaking, and when the outer circle, the outer circle is the ones who are selling the drugs, those who contribute and move drugs from city to city and community to community, and those who put them on drugs. So they exchange the goods for drugs.

GOVAN: And does that also include home invasions?
JULIAN: Yes, it's through the home invasions, house robberies..
GOVAN: But now we're talking about Despatch.. Why is it happening there?
JULIAN: They certainly have somebody who informed them was part of SAPS, who actually shared with them some information where there's police visibility or how many vehicles are despatched … which means they will know 30 minutes from now onwards. We will have 30 minutes to do the job here.
GOVAN: It's just because of police visibility.
JULIAN: there's a lack of vehicles, police visibility and in that certain precinct. And so I don't know what's wrong with the management of the police.
The Bay’s police crime stats are out of control - last year it had 80 murders per 100,000 people - above the national average.

Over the recent holidays - additional police officers were deployed.

With limited vehicles and officers at his disposal District Commissioner Major General Vuyisile Ncata adjusted SAPS members’ shifts to work at night.

COMM NCATA: We have taken everyone that are doing even administration work to go there and work because they are all police officers, because indeed we are really under pressure and watch the community is going through. It's not something that we want. And of course, as a district commissioner, I have a responsibility to ensure that Despatch is safe.

The border of the policing precinct that Despatch forms part of has also expanded.

COMM NCATA: There are other areas in the form of the informal settlements that were also added, you know, into the precinct of Despatch … that has made us also to stretch our resources because we must cover all areas…It does not mean that it's a situation that we cannot overcome.

GOVAN: Too much time… How much pressure are you under right now?

COMM NCATA: Too much. We are not sleeping. While working hard at work and that is why myself I am also involved in operations. Yes, I also work the streets as well.

What’s needed is smart policing - intelligence-driven dismantling of the groups that purchase the goods from robberies… and reduce murders during aggravated robberies.

Julian recruited many of the youngsters he’s now trying to save - young people like Jermaine who feel that in this economy it’s easier to get into a gang, than out of it.

Jermaine: That child won't hesitate to do it or he will be shot. He gets threatened. Do it now or never. That's how you become a gangster! It's as easy as that. You don't say: I want to be a gangster.
GOVAN: HOEKOM DIT DAT ‘N KLEIN LAITIE INGETREK WORD??
GERMAINE: Ingetrek vandag hulle op skool is.. Die kind gaan gedreig word.. Doen dit nou .. dit is hoe jy ‘n gangster raak - dit is hoe die ouers deel raak. 06 22 hulle kry die kinders wat mooi lyk - om in te breek… roof hulle… maklik soos dit.

Experts say the damage caused by the Bay’s gangs has too long been underestimated.
Late last year an elderly resident was getting ready for his shift when two intruders entered his garden. With his wife in the kitchen, he charged at them with a toy sword.
OLD MAN: I shone the flashlight at him and he told me “Stand still or I shoot.. The next minute he pulled the trigger - I thank our Father in heaven that he missed. They got the cartridge case that went to forensics. There was so much adrenaline.

GOVAN: Oom charged at them with a sword?.. with a gun in his hand?

OLD MAN: Yes, with the sword. I charged at them and they then ran around the pool.

GOVAN: Met die gun in die hand..

Pelting him with stones, pot plants and a panga - they nearly cut off his ear.
GOVAN: What did they steal?

OLD MAN: Just two cell phones.

GOVAN: Which almost cost Oom your life.

OLD MAN: But they want to kill you.

As Despatch beefs up security - the community has never been more united.

DARRYL: I don't like being a victim. And so I'm not going to allow them. And to chase me out of my home.

GOVAN: What do you have to say to the people you've hurt during the burglaries?
JERMAINE: 06 57 ons is moeg van dit
07 07 is ‘n plek vir in… nie ‘n plek vir uit nie… ek het niks meer toekoms nie - lewe vir nou
GOVAN: 11 17 wat se jy vir families?
GERMAINE: Hulle moet nie moed opgee nie..
12 12 se jammer vir die mense.. Ek is Germaine van die vyfde stop .. gebore hier gaan dood hier


PROMO 1
VO: Nelson Mandela Bay … on the edge….
Upsound Old Man: Thank the Lord in heaven the shot missed -the adrenaline was so much.
VO: Violent home invaders… terrorising communities … as the vicious cycle of gang criminality spreads to the rural outskirts.

PROMO 2
VO: It’s a metro under siege. Home robbery gangs are turning Nelson Mandela Bay upside down, leaving victims badly injured and some…dead.
Upsound Julian: A syndicate operating in the city which is unknown to them. So, they exchange the goods for drugs

PROMO 3
VO: A peaceful town ripped apart by violent home robberies …as Qgeberha’s gang activity spreads into new territory, leaving residents on the edge.
Upsound Daryll: Despatch has always been safe. If you had a break-in, It would most likely be someone that worked for you.

Why is it happening there? JULIAN: They certainly have somebody who informed them was part of SAPS, who actually shared with them some information where there's police visibility or how many vehicles are despatched … which means they will know 30 minutes from now onwards. We will have 30 minutes to do the job here. GOVAN: It's just because of police visibility. JULIAN: there's a lack of vehicles, police visibility and in that certain precinct. And so I don't know what's wrong with the management of the police. The Bay’s police crime stats are out of control - last year it had 80 murders per 100,000 people - above the national average. Over the recent holidays - additional police officers were deployed. With limited vehicles and officers at his disposal District Commissioner Major General Vuyisile Ncata adjusted SAPS members’ shifts to work at night. COMM NCATA: We have taken everyone that are doing even administration work to go there and work because they are all police officers, because indeed we are really under pressure and watch the community is going through. It's not something that we want. And of course, as a district commissioner, I have a responsibility to ensure that Despatch is safe. The border of the policing precinct that Despatch forms part of has also expanded. COMM NCATA: There are other areas in the form of the informal settlements that were also added, you know, into the precinct of Despatch … that has made us also to stretch our resources because we must cover all areas…It does not mean that it's a situation that we cannot overcome. GOVAN: Too much time… How much pressure are you under right now? COMM NCATA: Too much. We are not sleeping. While working hard at work and that is why myself I am also involved in operations. Yes, I also work the streets as well. What’s needed is smart policing - intelligence-driven dismantling of the groups that purchase the goods from robberies… and reduce murders during aggravated robberies. Julian recruited many of the youngsters he’s now trying to save - young people like Jermaine who feel that in this economy it’s easier to get into a gang, than out of it. Jermaine: That child won't hesitate to do it or he will be shot. He gets threatened. Do it now or never. That's how you become a gangster! It's as easy as that. You don't say: I want to be a gangster. GOVAN: HOEKOM DIT DAT ‘N KLEIN LAITIE INGETREK WORD?? GERMAINE: Ingetrek vandag hulle op skool is.. Die kind gaan gedreig word.. Doen dit nou .. dit is hoe jy ‘n gangster raak - dit is hoe die ouers deel raak. 06 22 hulle kry die kinders wat mooi lyk - om in te breek… roof hulle… maklik soos dit. Experts say the damage caused by the Bay’s gangs has too long been underestimated. Late last year an elderly resident was getting ready for his shift when two intruders entered his garden. With his wife in the kitchen, he charged at them with a toy sword. OLD MAN: I shone the flashlight at him and he told me “Stand still or I shoot.. The next minute he pulled the trigger - I thank our Father in heaven that he missed. They got the cartridge case that went to forensics. There was so much adrenaline. GOVAN: Oom charged at them with a sword?.. with a gun in his hand? OLD MAN: Yes, with the sword. I charged at them and they then ran around the pool. GOVAN: Met die gun in die hand.. Pelting him with stones, pot plants and a panga - they nearly cut off his ear. GOVAN: What did they steal? OLD MAN: Just two cell phones. GOVAN: Which almost cost Oom your life. OLD MAN: But they want to kill you. As Despatch beefs up security - the community has never been more united. DARRYL: I don't like being a victim. And so I'm not going to allow them. And to chase me out of my home. GOVAN: What do you have to say to the people you've hurt during the burglaries? JERMAINE: 06 57 ons is moeg van dit 07 07 is ‘n plek vir in… nie ‘n plek vir uit nie… ek het niks meer toekoms nie - lewe vir nou GOVAN: 11 17 wat se jy vir families? GERMAINE: Hulle moet nie moed opgee nie.. 12 12 se jammer vir die mense.. Ek is Germaine van die vyfde stop .. gebore hier gaan dood hier PROMO 1 VO: Nelson Mandela Bay … on the edge…. Upsound Old Man: Thank the Lord in heaven the shot missed -the adrenaline was so much. VO: Violent home invaders… terrorising communities … as the vicious cycle of gang criminality spreads to the rural outskirts. PROMO 2 VO: It’s a metro under siege. Home robbery gangs are turning Nelson Mandela Bay upside down, leaving victims badly injured and some…dead. Upsound Julian: A syndicate operating in the city which is unknown to them. So, they exchange the goods for drugs PROMO 3 VO: A peaceful town ripped apart by violent home robberies …as Qgeberha’s gang activity spreads into new territory, leaving residents on the edge. metadata.Summary: THE NB GANGS The community of Despatch, a small town just outside of Gqeberha in the Eastern Cape, sleeps with one eye open, living in fear as the notorious gang known as The Panga Gang has been terrorising them for months. They are known for striking in the early hours (between 2 am and 4 am) more especially during load shedding making off with home appliances and cell phones. Before, they used to carry pangas and screwdrivers but off late, they have added firearms. The Panga Gang is also accused or suspected of being responsible for the recent break-in at an old-age home in Bluewater Bay where two people were murdered and the killers making off with four phones, jewellery and two TV sets. Despatch is a community of just over 50 000 people with one police van. They describe the town as one of the most peaceful but now it expereinces at least 16 break-ins a week and shoes with shootings. The communities have now formed countless patrol groups and hit the streets every night and also use social media to alert the communities. They are installing cameras and some acquiring their own weapons. Headlines splashed in the local newspapers include “Robbery gangs strike fear in Nelson Mandela Bay”, “Robbery gangs target western suburbs”, “Panga Gang or copycats branching out into Despatch” However, this hasn’t discouraged the criminals and instead gave birth to two more gangs, The Balaclava Gang and the Quantum gang victimising the same neighbourhoods. This trend 2 am break-ins is currently spreading all over the Nelson Mandela Bay and has now included other towns like Kariega (Uitenhage), Bluewater Bay and other parts of Gqeberha. the story to investigate how this shocked community is dealing with this and steps they have taken to protect themselves.
